newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Hunn says SFO head investigation continuing.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Hunn says SFO head investigation continuing.

text.p: State Services Commissioner Don Hunn on Thursday assured parliament he had not swept under the carpet an investigation into whether Serious Fraud Office director Charles Sturt misled parliament.
"Certainly we have not brushed it under the carpet," top public servant Hunn told parliament's Government Administration select committee during an examination of the public service's performance.

Hunn, who is responsible for hiring and firing public service chief executives, said it may not be possible to release his findings until the release of the Davison "winebox" inquiry report into tax deals done through the Cook Islands tax haven during the 1980s.
Hunn told Reuters in an interview after the select committee hearing that the State Services Commission had begun examining Sturt's conduct.
"We have certainly started some work on that. We had to look at the transcript of the inquiry.
"We would have to look at Hansard and discuss those things with the relevant people. I would need to know what ministers thought was being said to them in the advice being given to them at the time."
During cross-examination at the Davison inquiry Sturt said there had been moves to hand documents back to tax scheme designer European Pacific.
In 1994 in a reply to a parliamentary question drafted by Sturt he said the SFO had not sought to hand the documents back.
"Mr Sturt is absolutely adamant he did not mislead parliament. He couldn't be more clear in his own mind about it," Hunn told Reuters.

"The question was asked of him on the day he was not well so there was some confusion on that day, but he has subsequently made it very clear both publicly and to me personally that he is sure in his own mind that he did not mislead parliament."
"Now there is some problem over the use of words and that is the bit I am examining," Hunn said.
Asked if he would make his findings public before the Davison commission issued its report, Hunn said: "Probably not, but I would have to take advice on that."
The winebox deals were brought to light by Treasurer Winston Peters when in opposition.
The Davison commission is required to establish if Inland Revenue and the Serious Fraud Office acted lawfully and competently in handling the documents. It is expected to report later this year.
